planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in early spring in full sun to part shade; Rubina is self-fertile and its vigorous upright habit benefits from 3-4 feet of spacing to accommodate heavy fruit clusters.

directions: Rubina is a Hungarian-bred black chokeberry selection resulting from a cross of 'Viking' with a Russian aronia variety, chosen for producing notably large berries and ripening earlier than most other black chokeberry cultivars. Its vigorous, upright growth habit yields heavy clusters of glossy black fruit that are slightly sweeter and less astringent than typical seed-grown Aronia melanocarpa, making them popular for fresh eating as well as juice, syrup, and jam. White flower clusters open in mid-spring and draw a wide range of pollinators before the summer foliage matures to deep green, then turns vivid orange-red in fall. Rubina tolerates wet or periodically saturated soils far better than most fruiting shrubs but performs poorly in shallow, chalky ground, so amend heavy alkaline soils before planting and mulch to retain even moisture.
sources: Ohio State University Extension — Growing Aronia in Ohio

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; Burkwood osmanthus tolerates shearing well, so it can be sited as a formal hedge or left to its naturally dense, rounded form.

directions: Burkwood osmanthus is a hybrid between Osmanthus delavayi and Osmanthus decorus that combines the small, deliciously fragrant white spring flowers of the former with the tougher constitution and glossy, finely toothed evergreen foliage of the latter. It forms a dense, rounded shrub that holds its shape with minimal pruning, making it a reliable choice for screening, foundation planting, or a clipped formal hedge, though it can also be limbed up into a small multi-stemmed tree. Flowering is heaviest in full sun, but the plant tolerates partial shade, heavy clay, alkaline soil, and urban pollution better than many broadleaf evergreens. Established plants are quite drought-tolerant, though supplemental water during dry spells improves flowering and keeps the foliage dense; avoid poorly drained sites since it will not tolerate standing water.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox
Royal Horticultural Society — Osmanthus x burkwoodii

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; Sasaba grows very slowly into a narrow upright column, making it well suited to tight side yards or narrow foundation beds where width is limited.

directions: Sasaba is a Japanese selection of holly osmanthus whose cultivar name means "bamboo leaf," describing its distinctive narrow, deeply lobed, spine-tipped leaves that radiate outward like slender bamboo foliage rather than the broader holly-like leaves of the species. It grows very slowly into a narrow, upright, columnar shrub, rarely spreading beyond about two feet wide even after many years, which makes it valuable for tight spaces where a wider osmanthus would not fit. Small, intensely fragrant white flowers open in fall and, unlike many holly osmanthus cultivars, Sasaba sometimes follows bloom with blue-black fruit. It grows well in partial shade to full sun and tolerates drought once established, though even moisture and protection from harsh winter wind keep the foliage looking its best.
sources: University of Washington Botanic Gardens — Plant Profile

common_name: Pink Lady Flowering Quince (Rich Pink Early-Spring Quince)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in any well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; Pink Lady forms a dense, bushy, thorny mound and blooms on old wood, so prune only immediately after flowering.

directions: Pink Lady is a flowering quince selection bearing rich, rose-pink, cup-shaped blossoms that open from darker pink buds in profusion along the thorny, leafless branches in late winter and early spring, ahead of most other flowering shrubs. Its dense, bushy, tangled habit spreads wider than it grows tall, giving it good presence as an informal hedge, barrier planting, or flowering specimen, and small, hard, yellow-green fruit follows the bloom in fall that can be used for jelly and preserves. It tolerates poor, clay, sandy, or alkaline soil and is quite drought-tolerant once established, asking for little beyond good drainage. Because flower buds form on the previous year's growth, prune only right after flowering finishes to avoid cutting off the next season's display.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society — Chaenomeles x superba 'Pink Lady'

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in reliably moist to wet soil; Keystone is a larger, more vigorous conservation-grade selection well suited to pond margins, wetland restoration, and rain gardens.

directions: Keystone was released in 1996 by the USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service and the Pennsylvania Game Commission as an improved buttonbush selection for conservation and wildlife plantings, chosen for greater vigor, larger size, and heavier flowering than typical seed-grown plants. Glossy dark green leaves back up round, creamy white, ball-shaped flower heads that open in mid to late summer and are heavily visited by bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds, followed by persistent seed balls that feed waterfowl and songbirds into winter. Like the species, Keystone tolerates standing water and periodic flooding better than nearly any other flowering shrub, making it an excellent choice for pond edges, bioswales, and low, poorly drained spots, though it also performs well in average moist garden soil. Fall color is a rich reddish-purple; prune hard in late winter if a more compact form is desired, since flowers form on new wood.
sources: USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service — Plant Materials Program

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; Bok Tower performs best in warm southern zones where winters stay mild and fruits most heavily with at least a half day of direct sun.

directions: Bok Tower is a white-fruited selection of native American beautyberry, discovered and introduced by Jonathan Shaw of Bok Tower Gardens in Polk County, Florida. In place of the species' vivid magenta-purple berries, its arching stems ring in late summer and fall with clusters of clean, pearly white fruit that stand out against the green foliage and offer a cooler-toned alternative for gardeners who want the beautyberry effect in a different palette. Small white flowers appear a bit later in summer than on typical beautyberry, tucked along the stems ahead of the fruit display, and the ripe berries are readily eaten by mockingbirds and other songbirds. It adapts to sand, loam, or clay as long as drainage is reasonable, and like other beautyberry selections, cutting the plant back hard in late winter encourages the vigorous new growth on which the heaviest fruit set depends.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox

common_name: Fire Dance Loropetalum (Deep Pink Burgundy-Leaf Fringe Flower)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Fire Dance holds its burgundy leaf color best with several hours of direct sun and can fade toward green in heavier shade.

directions: Fire Dance is a mid-sized Loropetalum chinense var. rubrum cultivar grown for its deep burgundy-purple foliage and abundant, deep pink, spidery-petaled flowers that open in a strong flush in early spring with lighter, sporadic rebloom through the growing season. Its rounded, moderately compact habit needs little pruning to stay tidy, making it useful as a mid-height hedge, mass planting, or mixed-border accent where its dark foliage contrasts well against green-leaved companions. Foliage color develops most intensely in full sun to light shade; in denser shade the leaves trend greener and flowering lightens. Once established, Fire Dance tolerates heat, humidity, and the clay soils common across the Gulf South, and needs only routine watering during dry spells to perform reliably.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society — Loropetalum chinense var. rubrum 'Fire Dance'
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Loropetalum
